title: Disaster Recovery Community Update Meeting #1 at Lahaina Civic Center: November 8, 2023

issues.title: Moving fire survivors off FEMA interim housing

recap.headline: First weekly Lahaina fire recovery update covers reentry, cleanup, insurance and housing
recap.in_60_seconds: County, state and federal agencies held the first of a planned weekly series of recovery updates at the Lahaina Civic Center. The Mayor opened, and Maui Emergency Management's administrator ran a program of short agency reports, with questions sent to breakout tables instead of an open mic. EPA said its hazardous material cleanup was 92 percent done and soil stabilizer work was about 34 percent done. The Army Corps explained right-of-entry debris removal, the Department of Health covered air and ash testing, the Insurance Commissioner reported claims paid, and FEMA described rental help that can run up to 18 months. One resident objected loudly to soil stabilizer being sprayed while owners were on their properties, and the emergency administrator said he would fix the coordination. Officials announced the SBA loan deadline had been extended into December and that meetings will continue every Wednesday at 5:30.

parts.title: Welcome and purpose of the meetings
presented: First of a series of community update meetings at the Lahaina Civic Center.
Ten more community sessions of about 40 people each are planned around Maui island.
The County is trying social media, newspapers and flyers to reach residents and asked which works best.
Members of the Mayor's Lahaina advisory team were named as resource people.

next.what: Ten community sessions of about 40 people each around Maui island

parts.title: Meeting format and reentry update
presented: Agencies will give updates, then answer questions at breakout tables instead of an open mic.
Reentry aims to let owners and residents see their parcels and settle insurance claims.
Work continues to return people to standing structures; one building at an entrance is at risk of collapse.
Many Lahaina zones still lack potable water; wastewater service was recently restored.

parts.title: EPA hazardous material cleanup and soil stabilizer
presented: Phase 1 hazardous material removal is 92 percent complete; residential parcels done by early next week, commercial by Thanksgiving.
Soil stabilizer work in Lahaina began mid-October and is about 34 percent done; Kula was finished in September.
People should wait 24 hours before disturbing ash where stabilizer was applied; no spraying 48 hours before or after a zone reopens.
Lithium-ion and lead-acid battery removal continues into early December, when EPA's mission ends.

raised.concern: A resident objected that soil stabilizer was being applied to properties while owners were there and called it unsafe and untested.

answered.said: EPA is committed to not applying soil stabilizer while people are on their properties and believes it makes returning safer by keeping ash from blowing.
He took responsibility and said he will fix the coordination problems with stabilizer application, working with EPA.

next.what: Soil stabilizer and battery work completed and EPA mission ends

parts.title: Army Corps debris removal process
parts.presenter: Commander, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Recovery Field Office, with a Corps subject matter expert
presented: A Corps call center opened that day, seven days a week from 6 a.m. to 6:30, plus a website showing each property's status.
Debris removal has started in Kula; Lahaina has site and archaeological assessments on every parcel first.
Owners sign a right of entry or do their own removal through Maui County's alternative program.
Owners get 72 hours' notice; metal and concrete are recycled, ash is wetted and hauled to a temporary site, and six inches of soil are removed and tested.

parts.title: Air quality, ash sampling and drinking water
parts.presenter: Deputy Director for Environmental Health, Hawaiʻi Department of Health
presented: 48 sensors and monitors are installed, with data from 20 real-time monitors in Lahaina posted online.
Yellow readings mean limit outdoor activity; recent odd readings came from a bird in a sensor and leaf blowing.
About 100 Lahaina homes will be sampled for heavy metals, PFAS and dioxins; air monitoring in Kula prepares for debris removal.
Restoring the full Lahaina water system under the unsafe water advisory will be a long process.

parts.title: Insurance claims update
presented: Insurers have paid about 85 percent of motor vehicle claims in the first three months.
About $670 million, roughly half of about $1.3 billion in property claims, has been paid.
Claims data will be updated every two weeks or monthly online.
A process now lets insurance adjusters apply to enter zones; staff are at the Disaster Recovery Center daily for questions and complaints.

parts.title: Future meeting topics
presented: Housing and final disposal of debris are planned for future meetings.
Meetings will be held on a regular Wednesday schedule.

next.what: Updates on housing and debris disposal

parts.title: FEMA housing assistance
presented: Over 3,400 people have received FEMA rental assistance, renewable in three-month increments up to 18 months.
FEMA raised the rate to 175 percent of fair market rent because local rents are high.
FEMA will lease vacation rentals directly and sublease them, with hundreds of units expected in the next couple of weeks.
Insured applicants must provide insurance settlement documents to complete applications.

next.what: Hundreds of directly leased units brought on

parts.title: Deadline extension and weekly schedule
presented: Thanks given to FEMA for extending the assistance deadline.
Meetings will be every Wednesday at 5:30 at the Civic Center with different agencies.

parts.title: SBA loan reminder and closing
presented: Apply for an SBA loan even if you don't plan to take it; a denial can trigger more FEMA aid.
SBA loans are 2.5 percent, up to $500,000 for a home and $100,000 for other items.
The SBA deadline, due the next day, was extended to December 8.

open_questions.question: How will soil stabilizer spraying be coordinated so it is not applied while owners are on their properties?
Where will Lahaina fire debris finally be disposed of?

not_on_tracker.why: A returning owner felt the spraying put people on their property at risk.

not_on_tracker.topic: Army Corps debris removal and right-of-entry forms
not_on_tracker.why: Owners must choose the Corps program or self-removal before cleanup of their lot.
Only about half of property claims had been paid, and adjusters needed zone access.

not_on_tracker.topic: Air quality and ash testing in Lahaina
not_on_tracker.why: Residents returning to burned areas need to know about health risks from ash and dust.
Applying, even if denied, can open more FEMA aid for survivors.
